concepts.name: Electricity in daily life
concepts.simple_answer: Electricity is a controllable, convenient form of energy used in homes, schools, hospitals and industries.
concepts.why: Most modern devices depend on electric circuits.
concepts.example: Lights, fans and phones all need electricity.

concepts.name: What is electric current?
concepts.simple_answer: When electric charge flows through a conductor (like a metallic wire), we say there is an electric current in it.
concepts.why: Current is moving charge — like water current in a river.
concepts.example: Torch bulb glows when charges flow through it.
concepts.remember: Flow of charge in conductor = current.

concepts.name: Electrons carry current in wires
concepts.simple_answer: In metallic wires, electrons constitute the flow of charges that make up electric current.
concepts.example: Copper wires in home circuits carry electron drift.
concepts.common_confusion: Current is not always positive charges in reality.

concepts.name: Conventional current direction
concepts.simple_answer: Conventionally, current direction is taken as opposite to electron flow — as if positive charges move from cell + to −.
concepts.why: Historical convention before electrons were known.
concepts.example: Arrow on circuit diagrams shows conventional current.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not draw electrons moving the same way as conventional arrow.

concepts.name: Electric circuit
concepts.simple_answer: A continuous and closed path for electric current is called an electric circuit.
concepts.example: Open switch → torch off; closed switch → bulb on.
concepts.remember: Closed loop needed for steady current.

concepts.name: Role of a switch
concepts.simple_answer: A switch makes or breaks the conducting link between the cell and the bulb (or other component).
concepts.why: Controls current without removing the cell.
concepts.example: Wall switch completes room light circuit.
concepts.remember: Switch ON = closed path; OFF = break.

concepts.name: Cell and battery in a torch
concepts.simple_answer: Cells (or a battery in proper order) provide flow of charges — current — through the torch bulb.
concepts.why: The source drives charge around the loop.
concepts.example: Two AA cells in series in a torch.

concepts.name: Circuit must be closed
concepts.simple_answer: If the circuit is broken anywhere, current stops and the bulb does not glow.

concepts.name: Rate of flow of charge
concepts.simple_answer: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charges through a cross-section: amount of charge per unit time.
concepts.why: Links measurable Q and t to current.
concepts.example: More charge passing per second = larger current.
concepts.common_confusion: I is not the same as total charge Q.

concepts.name: Water current analogy
concepts.simple_answer: Just as flowing water is water current, flowing electric charge is electric current.
concepts.common_confusion: Water and charge analogies break at atomic scale.

concepts.name: Current formula I = Q/t
concepts.simple_answer: If net charge Q flows across a cross-section in time t, current I = Q/t.
concepts.remember: I = Q/t; rearrange for Q = It.
concepts.common_confusion: Use t in seconds for SI.

concepts.name: Coulomb — unit of charge
concepts.simple_answer: SI unit of charge is coulomb (C). One coulomb equals charge of about 6 × 10¹⁸ electrons.
concepts.why: Connects electron charge to macroscopic Q.

concepts.name: Ampere — unit of current
concepts.simple_answer: One ampere (A) is flow of one coulomb of charge per second: 1 A = 1 C/s.
concepts.example: 2 A means 2 coulombs pass each second.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not write A as coulomb alone.

concepts.name: Milliampere and microampere
concepts.simple_answer: Small currents: 1 mA = 10⁻³ A; 1 µA = 10⁻⁶ A.
concepts.example: LED might draw a few mA.
concepts.remember: mA and µA for tiny currents.

concepts.name: Ammeter
concepts.simple_answer: An ammeter measures electric current. It is always connected in series in the circuit.
concepts.why: Must carry the current you measure.
concepts.example: Ammeter in series with bulb in Fig 11.1.
concepts.common_confusion: Never connect ammeter in parallel across battery.

concepts.name: Schematic diagram Fig 11.1
concepts.simple_answer: NCERT Fig 11.1: cell, bulb, ammeter and plug key in one closed loop.
concepts.why: Standard diagram to copy in exams.
concepts.example: Draw and label all four parts.
concepts.remember: Cell → bulb → ammeter → key → back to cell.

concepts.name: Current direction in diagram
concepts.simple_answer: In the diagram, conventional current flows from positive terminal of cell, through bulb and ammeter, back to negative terminal.
concepts.example: Arrow from + of cell through external circuit.

concepts.name: Example 11.1 idea
concepts.simple_answer: I = 0.5 A for t = 10 min = 600 s → Q = It = 300 C flows through the bulb.

concepts.name: Electrons vs convention revisited
concepts.simple_answer: Electrons move from − to + inside external wire, but we draw current from + to −.

concepts.name: What an electric circuit means
concepts.simple_answer: A circuit means a closed conducting path connecting source, switch, load and meters as needed.
concepts.example: Torch wiring is a simple circuit.

concepts.name: Potential difference drives current
concepts.simple_answer: Charges flow in a wire only if there is electric potential difference (electric pressure) along the conductor.
concepts.why: Like water flowing due to height difference.
concepts.example: Battery creates pressure difference for electrons.

concepts.name: Water pressure analogy
concepts.simple_answer: Water does not flow in a horizontal tube unless one end is at higher pressure — same idea for charge.
concepts.example: Tank at height pushes water through pipe.

concepts.name: Cell maintains PD
concepts.simple_answer: Chemical action in a cell generates potential difference across terminals even when no current is drawn.
concepts.example: Multimeter reads ~1.5 V on new dry cell.

concepts.name: Potential difference definition
concepts.simple_answer: PD between two points = work done per unit charge moved between them: V = W/Q.
concepts.example: Moving 2 C with 12 J work → V = 6 V.
concepts.common_confusion: W is work in joules, Q in coulombs.

concepts.name: Volt — unit of PD
concepts.simple_answer: One volt: 1 joule of work per coulomb — 1 V = 1 J/C.
concepts.example: 1 V between points means 1 J/C work.

concepts.name: Voltmeter
concepts.simple_answer: Potential difference is measured with a voltmeter connected in parallel across the two points.
concepts.why: Parallel so it doesn't redirect all current.
concepts.example: Voltmeter across bulb measures bulb PD.
concepts.common_confusion: Do not put voltmeter in series.

concepts.name: Work and charge Example 11.2
concepts.simple_answer: Q = 2 C across 12 V → W = VQ = 24 J of work done on the charge.
concepts.example: 6 V battery moving 1 C does 6 J work.

concepts.name: Battery expends energy
concepts.simple_answer: To maintain current, the cell keeps converting stored chemical energy — expending it in the circuit.
concepts.why: Source energy becomes heat/light/motion in load.
concepts.example: Battery runs down after long use.
concepts.remember: Cell supplies energy continuously while current flows.

concepts.name: Saying '1 V between points'
concepts.simple_answer: 1 V between two points means 1 J of work is done to move 1 C from one point to the other.
concepts.example: Every coulomb gains 1 J energy across 1 V.

concepts.name: Device maintaining PD
concepts.simple_answer: A cell or battery maintains potential difference across a conductor in a circuit.

concepts.name: Circuit diagram purpose
concepts.simple_answer: Schematic diagrams use standard symbols instead of realistic pictures — easier to draw and read.
concepts.example: Exam answers use symbols not sketches of bulbs.

concepts.name: Electric cell symbol
concepts.simple_answer: One cell: long line (+) and short thick line (−).

concepts.name: Battery symbol
concepts.simple_answer: Battery = combination of cells: multiple cell symbols in series.

concepts.name: Open and closed switch
concepts.simple_answer: Open key: gap in line. Closed key: filled dot or bridge showing connection.
concepts.example: Open plug key stops Ohm's law activity.

concepts.name: Wire, joint, crossing
concepts.simple_answer: Straight lines for wires; dot at junction; crossing without dot means no connection.
concepts.example: Crossing lines without dot don't connect.
concepts.remember: Dot = joined; crossing alone = not joined.

concepts.name: Bulb and resistor symbols
concepts.simple_answer: Bulb: circle with cross or filament symbol. Resistor: zig-zag or rectangle labelled R.
concepts.example: R marks nichrome wire in Ohm's law exp.

concepts.name: Rheostat symbol
concepts.simple_answer: Variable resistance / rheostat: resistor arrow through rectangle.
concepts.why: Used to change current without changing voltage source.

concepts.name: Ammeter and voltmeter symbols
concepts.simple_answer: Ammeter: A in circle, series. Voltmeter: V in circle, parallel.
concepts.why: Placement matters as much as symbol.
concepts.example: Redraw Q2 circuit with meters correctly.
concepts.remember: A in series; V in parallel.

concepts.name: Reading a full schematic
concepts.simple_answer: Trace closed path: source → switch → loads → back to source; add meters correctly.
concepts.remember: Trace loop; check switch and meters.

concepts.name: Drawing exam circuits
concepts.simple_answer: Use ruler, label components, show switch state and meter placement clearly.
concepts.example: 3 cells of 2 V, resistors 5 Ω, 8 Ω, 12 Ω in series.

concepts.name: Ohm's law statement
concepts.simple_answer: Potential difference V across a metallic conductor is directly proportional to current I through it, at constant temperature.
concepts.example: Double V → double I for ohmic conductor.
concepts.common_confusion: Ohm's law fails if temperature changes much.

concepts.name: V = IR form
concepts.simple_answer: From Ohm's law: V/I = constant = R, so V = IR.

concepts.name: Resistance R
concepts.simple_answer: R = V/I is resistance — property of conductor to resist charge flow. SI unit: ohm (Ω).
concepts.why: Higher R → less current for same V.

concepts.name: One ohm defined
concepts.simple_answer: 1 Ω: when V = 1 V produces I = 1 A through conductor.
concepts.example: Household small resistor values in ohms to kilohms.

concepts.name: V–I graph
concepts.simple_answer: Plot of V vs I for ohmic wire is straight line through origin — slope gives R.
concepts.why: Fig 11.3 straight line = Ohm's law verified.
concepts.example: V/I same for each row in Activity 11.1 table.
concepts.common_confusion: Line not through origin → check zero error.

concepts.name: Activity 11.1 pattern
concepts.simple_answer: Increase cells → both V and I increase; ratio V/I stays approximately constant.
concepts.example: Nichrome wire XY in circuit Fig 11.2.
concepts.remember: V/I constant for same wire at same temperature.

concepts.name: I = V/R
concepts.simple_answer: Current I = V/R — current inversely proportional to resistance for fixed voltage.
concepts.why: Thicker/shorter wire → lower R → higher I.
concepts.example: Same 6 V: 20 Ω lamp vs 4 Ω conductor different current.

concepts.name: Good conductor vs resistor
concepts.simple_answer: Same-size good conductor: low R; resistor: appreciable R; insulator: very high R.
concepts.example: Nichrome vs copper same size — different I.

concepts.name: Why components differ in current
concepts.simple_answer: Different components offer different resistance — electrons retarded differently.
concepts.example: Torch bulb vs 10 W bulb same voltage different I.

concepts.name: Temperature condition
concepts.simple_answer: Ohm's law holds provided temperature of conductor remains the same.
concepts.why: Filament heats up — R changes when glowing.
concepts.example: Cold vs hot bulb filament resistance differs.
concepts.remember: Constant temperature assumption for ideal Ohm's law.

concepts.name: Rheostat / variable resistance
concepts.simple_answer: Device to regulate current without changing voltage source — changes R in circuit.
concepts.example: Slide rheostat in Ohm's law experiment.

concepts.name: Length and resistance
concepts.simple_answer: For uniform wire, R ∝ l — double length doubles resistance (same material, same area).
concepts.why: Activity 11.3: ammeter halves when length doubles.

concepts.name: Area and resistance
concepts.simple_answer: R ∝ 1/A — thicker wire (larger cross-section) has lower resistance.
concepts.why: Thick wires used for high current.

concepts.name: Material affects resistance
concepts.simple_answer: Same length and area, different materials give different R — depends on resistivity ρ.
concepts.why: Copper vs nichrome comparison in activity.
concepts.example: Copper wire vs nichrome same dimensions.

concepts.name: Combined proportionality
concepts.simple_answer: R ∝ l and R ∝ 1/A combined: R = ρ l / A.
concepts.example: Double length and halve area → R × 4.

concepts.name: Resistivity ρ
concepts.simple_answer: ρ (rho) is constant for material; SI unit Ω m. Characteristic property.
concepts.example: Silver low ρ; rubber very high ρ.
concepts.remember: ρ in Ω m; material property.

concepts.name: Conductors vs insulators
concepts.simple_answer: Metals/alloys: ρ ~ 10⁻⁸–10⁻⁶ Ω m (conductors). Rubber/glass: ~10¹²–10¹⁷ Ω m (insulators).
concepts.example: Copper for wires; rubber for insulation.
concepts.remember: Low ρ = conductor; high ρ = insulator.

concepts.name: Alloys vs pure metals
concepts.simple_answer: Alloys usually higher ρ than constituent metals; resist oxidation at high temperature.
concepts.why: Used in heating elements and nichrome.
concepts.example: Nichrome in heater; tungsten in bulb.
concepts.common_confusion: Alloy ρ higher but stable at heat.

concepts.name: Example 11.5 scaling
concepts.simple_answer: Same material: l halved and A doubled → R becomes 1/4 of original (4 Ω → 1 Ω).
concepts.example: Track l and A factors separately.

concepts.name: Thick vs thin wire question
concepts.simple_answer: Thick wire of same material conducts more easily — lower R, more current from same source.

concepts.name: Resistors in series — layout
concepts.simple_answer: Resistors connected end to end between same path — same current through each.
concepts.why: Fig 11.6 three resistors in one loop.

concepts.name: Same current in series
concepts.simple_answer: In series combination, current is same through every resistor and every part of circuit.
concepts.example: Ammeter before or after R₂ same reading.
concepts.common_confusion: Current is NOT shared in series.

concepts.name: PD adds in series
concepts.simple_answer: Total PD across series combination equals sum of PDs across individual resistors: V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃.
concepts.example: 6 V battery split across lamp and resistor.

concepts.name: Equivalent series resistance
concepts.simple_answer: Rₛ = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ — series equivalent greater than any single resistor.
concepts.example: 20 Ω lamp + 4 Ω resistor → 24 Ω total.

concepts.name: Example 11.7 outline
concepts.simple_answer: Lamp 20 Ω + conductor 4 Ω on 6 V: R=24 Ω, I=0.25 A, V₁=5 V, V₂=1 V.
concepts.example: Total R first, then I = V/R, then each V=IR.
concepts.remember: Series numerical: add R, find I, split V.

concepts.name: Resistors in parallel — layout
concepts.simple_answer: Resistors connected between same two points X and Y — same PD across each branch.
concepts.example: Home lights in parallel across mains.

concepts.name: Current splits in parallel
concepts.simple_answer: Total current equals sum of branch currents: I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃.
concepts.common_confusion: Current is NOT same in parallel branches.

concepts.name: Same PD in parallel
concepts.simple_answer: Potential difference across each parallel resistor equals PD across the combination.
concepts.why: Each appliance gets full mains PD (ideal).
concepts.example: 12 V across each of R₁, R₂, R₃ in Ex 11.8.
concepts.remember: Same V on each parallel branch.

concepts.name: Parallel equivalent formula
concepts.simple_answer: 1/Rₚ = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃ — equivalent R less than smallest individual.

concepts.name: Example 11.8 idea
concepts.simple_answer: 5 Ω, 10 Ω, 30 Ω parallel on 12 V: each branch I = V/R; total I = sum; Rₚ = 3 Ω.
concepts.example: I₁=2.4 A, I₂=1.2 A, I₃=0.4 A, total 4 A.
concepts.remember: Each V/R then add I; then find Rₚ.

concepts.name: Series R greater than parts
concepts.simple_answer: Series equivalent resistance is greater than any individual resistance.
concepts.why: More resistors in series → harder for current.
concepts.example: Adding 4 Ω to lamp increases total R.

concepts.name: Parallel R less than smallest
concepts.simple_answer: Parallel equivalent is less than the smallest individual resistance.
concepts.why: More parallel paths → easier overall flow.
concepts.example: Two equal resistors parallel → half each value.

concepts.name: Series impractical at home
concepts.simple_answer: Series circuit: same current everywhere — one failure breaks all; not used for household appliances.
concepts.why: NCERT explains why homes use parallel.
concepts.example: Old series fairy lights all off if one bulb fails.

concepts.name: Parallel domestic advantage
concepts.simple_answer: Each appliance gets full PD; independent switching; one branch off doesn't stop others.
concepts.why: Why fridge and TV work independently.
concepts.example: Turn off kitchen light — TV still on.

concepts.name: Mixed circuits strategy
concepts.simple_answer: Replace parallel groups by equivalent R, then add series parts (Example 11.9 method).
concepts.example: R′ for parallel pair, R″ for triple, then add.

concepts.name: Heating effect intro
concepts.simple_answer: When current flows through resistor, source energy dissipated as heat — heating effect of current.
concepts.why: Fan warm, heater hot — same physics.
concepts.example: Electric iron gets hot on current.

concepts.name: Power P = VI
concepts.simple_answer: Rate of energy: P = VI — electric power in watts.

concepts.name: Heat H = VIt
concepts.simple_answer: Energy (heat) in time t: H = VIt.

concepts.name: Joule's law H = I²Rt
concepts.simple_answer: Heat produced H = I²Rt — directly ∝ I², R, and t.

concepts.name: P = I²R and P = V²/R
concepts.simple_answer: Equivalent power forms: P = I²R = V²/R.
concepts.example: Known V and R → P = V²/R.

concepts.name: Watt unit
concepts.simple_answer: 1 watt = 1 joule per second = power when 1 A flows at 1 V.

concepts.name: Kilowatt and kWh
concepts.simple_answer: 1 kW = 1000 W. Commercial energy unit: kilowatt-hour (kWh) — 'unit' on electricity bill.

concepts.name: We pay for energy not electrons
concepts.simple_answer: Electricity bill charges for energy to move electrons through devices — not for consuming electrons.
concepts.example: Electrons circulate; energy is converted at load.

concepts.name: Electric iron power Example
concepts.simple_answer: 840 W max and 360 W min at 220 V → different I and R settings.
concepts.remember: P = VI gives I; R = V/I.

concepts.name: Heating element glows
concepts.simple_answer: Heating element high R, high heat; connecting cord low R — cord doesn't glow.
concepts.example: Nichrome coil hot; copper wire cool.
concepts.remember: Heat ∝ R; element designed for heat.

concepts.name: Bulb filament
concepts.simple_answer: Tungsten filament high melting point (3380°C), thermally isolated, in inactive gas.
concepts.why: Most power becomes heat; small part light.
concepts.remember: Tungsten + gas fill for bulb life.

concepts.name: Fuse protection
concepts.simple_answer: Fuse wire in series melts when current too high — breaks circuit, protects appliances.
concepts.why: Rated 1 A, 5 A, etc. for domestic use.
concepts.example: 1 kW iron at 220 V needs ~5 A fuse.

concepts.name: Choosing fuse rating
concepts.simple_answer: Fuse slightly above normal operating current — e.g. 5 A fuse for ~4.5 A appliance.
concepts.remember: Fuse rating > normal I but < dangerous I.

concepts.name: Heating applications
concepts.simple_answer: Electric iron, toaster, oven, kettle, heater use Joule heating deliberately.
concepts.why: Useful conversion of electrical to thermal energy.
concepts.remember: Joule heat for cooking and warmth.

concepts.name: Undesirable heating
concepts.simple_answer: Unwanted heat in motors/wires wastes energy and can damage components.

concepts.name: Ohm's law numerical pattern
concepts.simple_answer: Given any two of V, I, R find the third using V=IR or R=V/I.

concepts.name: Example 11.3 bulbs vs heater
concepts.simple_answer: Same 220 V: 1200 Ω bulb draws 0.18 A; 100 Ω heater draws 2.2 A.
concepts.why: Lower R → higher I at same V.
concepts.remember: Same V: small R → large I.

concepts.name: Example 11.4 doubling V
concepts.simple_answer: If R fixed, doubling V doubles I (60 V,4 A → 120 V,8 A when R=15 Ω).
concepts.example: Heater on higher setting if R unchanged.

concepts.name: Resistivity numerical
concepts.simple_answer: ρ = RA/l; use consistent metres for l and A (A = πd²/4).
concepts.example: R=26 Ω, l=1 m, d=0.3 mm → manganese.
concepts.remember: Convert mm² to m² for A.

concepts.name: Half PD half current
concepts.simple_answer: If R constant and V halved, I halves (NCERT Q3 resistors section).
concepts.remember: V halved → I halved if R fixed.

concepts.name: Series voltmeter reading Q
concepts.simple_answer: V across 12 Ω in series with 5 Ω and 8 Ω on 6 V three-cell: find I then V=IR.
concepts.example: Total R=25 Ω, I=6/25 A, V₁₂=IR.
concepts.remember: Series: total R, then split V.

concepts.name: Parallel branch currents
concepts.simple_answer: Each parallel I = V/R_branch; total I sum.

concepts.name: Heat from charge
concepts.simple_answer: Q through PD: H = VQ; 96000 C through 50 V in 1 h gives energy.
concepts.remember: H = VQ when all charge moved.

concepts.name: Heat in 30 s
concepts.simple_answer: H = I²Rt: 5 A through 20 Ω for 30 s → H = 15000 J.

concepts.name: Motor power Q
concepts.simple_answer: P = VI; energy = P × t. 5 A at 220 V → P = 1100 W.
concepts.example: 2 h energy = 1100 W × 7200 s or kWh method.

concepts.name: Tungsten for filament
concepts.simple_answer: High melting point prevents melt at glowing temperature.

concepts.name: Nichrome in heaters
concepts.simple_answer: Nichrome alloy high ρ, resists oxidation at red heat.

concepts.name: Copper for transmission
concepts.simple_answer: Low ρ copper/aluminium for power lines — minimal energy loss as heat.
concepts.example: Thick copper wires from pole to home.

concepts.name: Insulator role
concepts.simple_answer: Rubber/plastic insulation prevents accidental contact — very high ρ.

concepts.name: Temperature and ρ
concepts.simple_answer: Both R and ρ vary with temperature — mention when filament heats.
concepts.example: Bulb inrush current when switched on.

concepts.name: Activity 11.2 summary
concepts.simple_answer: Same voltage, different components → different I because R differs.
concepts.example: Swap nichrome, torch bulb, 10 W bulb.

concepts.name: Activity 11.3 summary
concepts.simple_answer: Vary l, A, material separately — observe ammeter change.
concepts.remember: l up → I down; A up → I up.

concepts.name: Series same I proof idea
concepts.simple_answer: Charge conservation: same current through series elements each second.

concepts.name: Parallel same V idea
concepts.simple_answer: Wires connect same two points → same potential difference.
concepts.example: Both ends of each R at X and Y.

concepts.name: Equivalent resistor concept
concepts.simple_answer: Single R that replaces network giving same V and I from source.

concepts.name: Draw series circuit exam
concepts.simple_answer: Battery + key + ammeter + resistors in one loop; voltmeter across one resistor.
concepts.example: Label each R and cell emf.

concepts.name: Ammeter placement
concepts.simple_answer: Always series — carries full circuit current.

concepts.name: Voltmeter placement
concepts.simple_answer: Always parallel across component whose PD you need.

concepts.name: Three resistors 6 Ω each
concepts.simple_answer: Can make 9 Ω series, 2 Ω parallel, or mixed — NCERT exercise Q11.
concepts.remember: Same R different connections → different R_eq.

concepts.name: Series PD division
concepts.simple_answer: V_i = I R_i; larger R gets larger share of voltage in series.
concepts.why: Lamp 20 Ω gets more V than 4 Ω on same I.
concepts.remember: Big R → big V drop in series.

concepts.name: Parallel current division
concepts.simple_answer: I_i = V/R_i; smaller R branch takes more current.
concepts.why: 5 Ω branch takes more I than 30 Ω at same V.
concepts.example: Low R path draws more I.

concepts.name: Two resistors parallel shortcut
concepts.simple_answer: R_eq = R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂) for two in parallel only.

concepts.name: Energy unit conversion
concepts.simple_answer: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J — use for cost problems.
concepts.remember: Convert W and hours to kWh.

concepts.name: Purely resistive circuit
concepts.simple_answer: If only resistors connected to battery, source energy all dissipated as heat.
concepts.example: Theoretical 100% heat in ideal R circuit.

concepts.name: Define electric current exam
concepts.simple_answer: Rate of flow of electric charge through a cross-section.

concepts.name: Define potential difference exam
concepts.simple_answer: Work done per unit charge moved between two points.

concepts.name: State Ohm's law exam
concepts.simple_answer: V ∝ I for metallic conductor at constant temperature; V = IR.

concepts.name: State Joule's law exam
concepts.simple_answer: H = I²Rt; heat ∝ I², R, and t.

concepts.name: Series vs parallel summary table
concepts.simple_answer: Series: same I, V adds, R adds. Parallel: same V, I adds, 1/R adds.
concepts.remember: Four rows: I, V, R, domestic use.

concepts.name: Why alloy in toaster
concepts.simple_answer: Higher ρ than pure metal; does not oxidise quickly at high temperature.
concepts.example: Nichrome coils stay stable when hot.

concepts.name: Better conductor iron or mercury
concepts.simple_answer: Iron (lower ρ than mercury in Table 11.2).

concepts.name: Best conductor in table
concepts.simple_answer: Silver lowest ρ (~1.60×10⁻⁸ Ω m) — best conductor listed.

concepts.name: Electrons per coulomb
concepts.simple_answer: 1 C ≈ 6×10¹⁸ electrons (each 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C).

concepts.name: Circuit broken at switch
concepts.simple_answer: Open switch → open circuit → no continuous path → I = 0.

concepts.name: Long answer: Ohm's law experiment
concepts.simple_answer: Describe Activity 11.1: vary cells, measure V and I, plot straight line, R = V/I constant.

concepts.name: Long answer: factors affecting R
concepts.simple_answer: State l, A, material; R = ρl/A; describe Activity 11.3 observations.

concepts.name: Long answer: series combination
concepts.simple_answer: Derive R_s = R₁+R₂, same I, V = V₁+V₂ with diagram Fig 11.6.

concepts.name: Long answer: parallel combination
concepts.simple_answer: Derive 1/R_p = sum of reciprocals; same V; I = I₁+I₂.

concepts.name: Long answer: heating effect
concepts.simple_answer: Explain H = I²Rt, energy source to heat, examples iron/bulb/fuse.

concepts.name: Long answer: electric power
concepts.simple_answer: Define P = VI, watt, kWh, billing example.

concepts.name: MCQ: maintains PD
concepts.simple_answer: Cell/battery maintains potential difference — not ammeter or resistor alone.

concepts.name: MCQ: image at retina wrong unit
concepts.simple_answer: Trap from other chapter — eye forms image at retina; electricity Q: image not here.

concepts.name: MCQ: ciliary muscles wrong chapter
concepts.simple_answer: Lens focal change is eye unit — electricity uses rheostat for variable R.

concepts.name: Safety: fuse and overload
concepts.simple_answer: Too high current melts fuse, stops fire risk from overheated wires.
concepts.example: Never replace fuse with higher rating wire.

concepts.name: Chapter map
concepts.simple_answer: Ch 11: current → PD → symbols → Ohm → R factors → series/parallel → heat → power.

concepts.name: Link to prior physics
concepts.simple_answer: Energy W = VQ connects to work and power from earlier classes.
concepts.remember: Electric energy follows same power idea.

concepts.name: Graph skills V–I
concepts.simple_answer: Slope ΔV/ΔI = R for ohmic conductor; intercept should be zero.

concepts.name: Unit analysis check
concepts.simple_answer: Verify formulas dimensionally: V/I → Ω; VI → W.
concepts.example: Wrong unit in answer flags mistake.

concepts.name: Series lamp dimmer
concepts.simple_answer: More resistors in series → higher R → lower I → lamp dimmer.

concepts.name: Parallel lamp independence
concepts.simple_answer: Parallel branch off → others unchanged brightness.
concepts.example: One bulb removed others stay on.

concepts.name: High power low resistance heater
concepts.simple_answer: Heater low R (100 Ω) draws large I at 220 V → high P = VI.
concepts.example: P = V²/R shows low R → high P.

concepts.name: Low power high resistance bulb
concepts.simple_answer: Bulb filament high R limits current → moderate power for light.
concepts.why: Designed for light not max heat.

concepts.name: Resistivity does not depend on shape
concepts.simple_answer: ρ is material property; R depends on l and A.
concepts.example: Thicker wire same material same ρ.
